title: Deploying Models with Streamlit
summary: A model sitting in a notebook helps no one; deployment is how you put it in front of users so it delivers value, and Streamlit is the fastest way for a data scientist to do this without web development experience. The workflow is: train your model, s
content:
# Deploying Models with Streamlit ##### The model that sat in a notebook for eight months A data scientist at an agritech company in Nashik built a crop-disease classifier. Validation accuracy: 94%. She presented it, the team was impressed, and the notebook went into a shared drive. Eight months later nobody had used it once. The field officers who needed it had no Python, no Jupyter, and no way to feed a photograph into a `.ipynb` file. She spent one afternoon building a Streamlit app — upload a photo, see the prediction and confidence, read a short explanation. She deployed it to a free URL and shared the link on the team WhatsApp group. In the first month it was used 340 times. The model never changed. What changed was **access**. A model in a notebook produces zero value regardless of its accuracy, and the gap between "it works in my notebook" and "someone can use it" is often a single afternoon that nobody schedules. ##### Why deployment matters Deployment is the step where a model stops being an analysis and becomes a product. Three things it forces you to confront that a notebook lets you avoid: - **Real inputs.** A user will enter an age of 250, leave a field blank, and upload a PDF where you expected a JPEG. - **The interpretation problem.** A number like 0.73 means nothing to a non-technical user without framing. - **The full transformation chain.** Every preprocessing step must be reproduced identically at prediction time, or the model receives data unlike anything it trained on. That third point is why yesterday's pipelines matter so much today. The deployment options, and where Streamlit sits: | Option | Effort | Good for | Limitation | |---|---|---|---| | **Streamlit** | Hours | Demos, internal tools, portfolios | Not for high-traffic APIs | | **Gradio** | Hours | ML demos, especially image and text | Less layout control | | **FastAPI** | Days | Production APIs, system integration | No UI; needs a frontend | | **Cloud endpoints** | Days | Enterprise scale, managed infra | Cost, complexity | For a data scientist who wants a working, shareable product this week, Streamlit is the right answer. ##### Saving and loading the model The critical rule: **save the whole pipeline, not just the estimator.** ```python import joblib from pathlib import Path from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier import json, datetime, sklearn num_cols = ["tenure_months", "monthly_charges", "total_charges", "age"] cat_cols = ["contract_type", "payment_method", "city"] pipe = Pipeline([ ("prep", ColumnTransformer([ ("num", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("sc", StandardScaler())]), num_cols), ("cat", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value="__missing__")), ("ohe", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"))]), cat_cols), ])), ("model", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=42, class_weight="balanced")), ]) pipe.fit(X_train, y_train) Path("models").mkdir(exist_ok=True) joblib.dump(pipe, "models/churn_pipeline.joblib", compress=3) # Metadata is not optional json.dump({ "sklearn_version": sklearn.__version__, "trained_at": datetime.datetime.now().isoformat(), "numeric_features": num_cols, "categorical_features": cat_cols, "categories": {c: sorted(X_train[c].dropna().unique().tolist()) for c in cat_cols}, "test_auc": round(float(pipe.score(X_test, y_test)), 4), "threshold": 0.35, }, open("models/metadata.json", "w"), indent=2) ``` Saving only `RandomForestClassifier` means re-implementing the scaler and encoder in the app — and getting them subtly different, which produces a model that runs fine and predicts nonsense. The pipeline carries every learned parameter with it. The `categories` field in the metadata is a practical touch: it lets the app populate dropdowns with exactly the values the model was trained on, so users cannot enter something unseen. Two cautions. **Pin `scikit-learn`** in your requirements and record the version — a mismatch produces warnings at best and silent misbehaviour at worst. And **never load a `.joblib` from an untrusted source**, since pickle executes code on load. ##### Building the Streamlit app ```python # app.py import streamlit as st import pandas as pd import joblib, json from pathlib import Path st.set_page_config(page_title="Churn Risk Predictor", page_icon="📊", layout="centered") @st.cache_resource # cache_resource for models, not cache_data def load_model(): return (joblib.load("models/churn_pipeline.joblib"), json.load(open("models/metadata.json"))) model, meta = load_model() st.title("Customer Churn Risk") st.caption(f"Model trained {meta['trained_at'][:10]} · " f"Test AUC {meta['test_auc']} · For internal use") with st.form("prediction_form"): st.subheader("Customer details") c1, c2 = st.columns(2) with c1: tenure = st.number_input("Tenure (months)", 0, 240, 12, step=1, help="How long they have been a customer") monthly = st.number_input("Monthly charges (₹)", 0.0, 100_000.0, 1200.0, step=50.0) age = st.number_input("Age", 18, 100, 35) with c2: contract = st.selectbox("Contract type", meta["categories"]["contract_type"]) payment = st.selectbox("Payment method", meta["categories"]["payment_method"]) city = st.selectbox("City", meta["categories"]["city"]) submitted = st.form_submit_button("Predict", type="primary", use_container_width=True) if submitted: total = monthly * max(tenure, 1) row = pd.DataFrame([{ "tenure_months": tenure, "monthly_charges": monthly, "total_charges": total, "age": age, "contract_type": contract, "payment_method": payment, "city": city, }]) prob = float(model.predict_proba(row)[0, 1]) threshold = meta["threshold"] st.divider() left, right = st.columns([1, 2]) with left: st.metric("Churn probability", f"{prob:.1%}") with right: if prob >= 0.60: st.error("**High risk** — recommend immediate retention outreach") elif prob >= threshold: st.warning("**Moderate risk** — include in the next retention campaign") else: st.success("**Low risk** — no action needed") st.progress(prob) with st.expander("How to read this"): st.markdown(f""" This score estimates the probability that this customer cancels within the next 90 days, based on patterns in {meta.get('n_train', '80,000+')} historical customers. - **Above 60%** — high risk, act now - **{threshold:.0%} to 60%** — moderate, include in campaigns - **Below {threshold:.0%}** — low risk The score is a *statistical estimate*, not a certainty. It should inform a decision, not make one. Model AUC on held-out data: {meta['test_auc']}. """) ``` ```bash streamlit run app.py ``` Three design choices worth highlighting. **`st.form`** batches the inputs so the model runs once when the user clicks Predict, rather than re-running on every keystroke. Without it, a form with six widgets triggers six predictions as someone fills it in. **`@st.cache_resource`** loads the model once per session rather than on every interaction. Use `cache_resource` for unpickled objects like models and database connections, and `cache_data` for DataFrames. **The interpretation section** is what makes this usable by a non-technical person. A bare "0.73" is not a product; "Moderate risk — include in the next retention campaign" is. ##### Input validation Users will enter impossible values. Handle it explicitly rather than letting the model extrapolate silently. ```python def validate(row: dict, meta: dict) -> list[str]: problems = [] if row["tenure_months"] > 240: problems.append("Tenure over 20 years is outside the training range.") if row["monthly_charges"] <= 0: problems.append("Monthly charges must be greater than zero.") if row["age"] < 18: problems.append("Model is only validated for adults (18+).") if row["monthly_charges"] > 50_000: problems.append("Charges above ₹50,000 are outside the training range — " "treat this prediction with caution.") return problems if submitted: issues = validate(row.iloc[0].to_dict(), meta) if issues: for msg in issues: st.warning(msg) # Decide: block, or predict with a caveat if any("must be" in m for m in issues): st.stop() ``` The distinction that matters: **out-of-range is a warning; impossible is a hard stop.** A model asked to predict for a customer with 40 years of tenure when training data topped out at 20 will produce a number, and that number is unsupported extrapolation. Telling the user is honest; refusing outright is often too strict. Wrapping the prediction itself: ```python try: prob = float(model.predict_proba(row)[0, 1]) except Exception as e: st.error("Prediction failed. Please check your inputs.") st.exception(e) # remove or gate this in production st.stop() ``` ##### Batch predictions and explanations Two additions that substantially raise the usefulness of an internal tool: ```python st.divider() st.subheader("Score a batch") uploaded = st.file_uploader("Upload a CSV", type="csv") if uploaded: batch = pd.read_csv(uploaded) required = meta["numeric_features"] + meta["categorical_features"] missing = set(required) - set(batch.columns) if missing: st.error(f"Missing required columns: {sorted(missing)}") else: batch["churn_probability"] = model.predict_proba(batch[required])[:, 1] batch["risk"] = pd.cut(batch["churn_probability"], bins=[0, meta["threshold"], 0.60, 1.0], labels=["Low", "Moderate", "High"]) st.dataframe(batch.sort_values("churn_probability", ascending=False), use_container_width=True) st.download_button("Download scored CSV", batch.to_csv(index=False), "scored_customers.csv", "text/csv") st.bar_chart(batch["risk"].value_counts()) ``` And a per-prediction explanation, which turns a black box into something a user can act on: ```python import shap @st.cache_resource def get_explainer(_model): return shap.TreeExplainer(_model.named_steps["model"]) if submitted and st.checkbox("Show what drove this prediction"): prep = model.named_steps["prep"] transformed = prep.transform(row) names = prep.get_feature_names_out() sv = get_explainer(model).shap_values(transformed) contrib = pd.Series(sv[1][0] if isinstance(sv, list) else sv[0], index=names) top = contrib.reindex(contrib.abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index).head(6) st.bar_chart(top) st.caption("Positive bars increase churn risk; negative bars reduce it.") ``` ##### Deploying to Streamlit Community Cloud ```bash pip freeze > requirements.txt git init git add app.py requirements.txt models/ .gitignore git commit -m "Add churn prediction Streamlit app" git remote add origin https://github.com/yourname/churn-app.git git push -u origin main ``` Then connect the repository at `share.streamlit.io`, point it at `app.py`, and deploy. It gives you a public URL in a couple of minutes. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Train pipeline
in notebook] --> B[joblib.dump
pipeline + metadata] B --> C[Write app.py
widgets + load + predict] C --> D[Test locally
streamlit run app.py] D --> E[requirements.txt
pinned versions] E --> F[Push to GitHub] F --> G[Deploy on
Streamlit Cloud] G --> H[Share the URL] ``` Practical requirements for deployment to succeed: - **Pin every version** in `requirements.txt`, especially `scikit-learn`. A version mismatch between training and serving is the most common deployment failure. - **Commit the model file** if it is small (under about 50 MB). Larger models should be downloaded at startup from cloud storage. - **Secrets go in app settings**, never in code: `st.secrets["DB_URL"]`. - **Free tier apps sleep** after inactivity and take 30 seconds to wake. Mention this if you share the link on a CV. - **Public means public.** Never deploy an app exposing real customer data to a public URL. Use authentication and a private deployment for anything real. ```python # Minimal password gate for internal tools def check_password(): if st.session_state.get("authenticated"): return True pwd = st.text_input("Password", type="password") if pwd and pwd == st.secrets["APP_PASSWORD"]: st.session_state["authenticated"] = True return True elif pwd: st.error("Incorrect password") return False if not check_password(): st.stop() ``` ##### Common mistakes - Saving only the estimator, then re-implementing preprocessing in the app. - Version mismatch between the training and serving environments. - No `st.cache_resource`, reloading the model on every interaction. - No form, so the model runs on every keystroke. - No input validation, so the model extrapolates silently on impossible values. - A raw probability shown with no interpretation. - No handling for unseen categorical values (fix it with `handle_unknown="ignore"`). - Secrets or a database URL committed in the code. - Real customer data on a public URL. - Building the app and never testing it with an actual non-technical user. ##### Hands-on Save a trained pipeline with `joblib` alongside a metadata JSON, then build a Streamlit app that takes user input through widgets, loads the model with `@st.cache_resource`, and displays a live prediction inside a form. Run it locally and deliberately try to break it — leave a field at zero, enter an extreme value, and confirm each produces a helpful message rather than a stack trace or a silently absurd prediction. For the mini-project, deploy one of your models as a public Streamlit app end to end: build the interface, add input validation with clear messages, include a batch-upload path with a downloadable scored CSV, write an interpretation section a non-technical reader can follow, push to GitHub with pinned requirements, and deploy to Streamlit Community Cloud. Then add the link to your README and your CV. A working URL that a hiring manager can click is worth substantially more than a notebook they will not open. For the assignment, add input validation and a clear explanation of the prediction to your app so a non-technical user understands the result. Then test that claim properly — give the link to someone with no data science background, watch them use it without guidance, and note every point where they hesitated or misread something. Those observations are the actual deliverable. ##### Key takeaways - A model in a notebook delivers zero value; deployment is what converts accuracy into impact. - Save the entire pipeline plus metadata — re-implementing preprocessing at serving time is how models silently break. - Use `@st.cache_resource` for the model and `st.form` to batch inputs, or the app reruns constantly. - Validate inputs explicitly: warn on out-of-range, block on impossible, and never extrapolate silently. - Translate the probability into an action, pin your versions, keep secrets out of code, and never expose real data publicly.
